core: working definition: identity theft is when someone uses another person's personal or financial information without permission, usually for money (attributed to FTC)
how it happens: data breaches, phishing, stolen mail, and card skimmers — each named with one line and an original example
warning signs: unexpected bills, unfamiliar accounts, and being denied credit you expected — each named
protecting information: strong passwords, shredding documents, and guarding the Social Security number — general practice, stated simply
if it happens: report, freeze, dispute — the general recovery steps named, attributed to FTC; no legal advice
identity theft and credit: fraud can damage credit reports — the link; credit-reports is a sibling topic
honest framing: identity theft is a crime of access, not of trust — the reality check
supporting: what thieves do with stolen information: buy things, open cards and utility accounts, rent apartments, collect benefits or refunds
data-breach response guidance: act quickly on breach notices, change reused passwords, turn on extra login security
credit freeze mechanics: blocks new credit accounts, free to place and lift, does not affect the credit score
fraud alert mechanics: businesses must verify identity before opening new credit; initial alert lasts one year
the free annual credit report and the free report after a denial based on the report
IdentityTheft.gov as the federal one-stop resource that generates a personal recovery plan

claims.claim: The FTC defines identity theft as when someone uses your personal or financial information without your permission; the information targeted includes name and address, credit card or bank account numbers, Social Security number, and medical insurance account numbers.

The CFPB frames identity theft as occurring when someone steals your identity to commit fraud — using personal information without permission — and thieves may rent apartments, get credit cards, receive government benefits or tax refunds, or open other accounts in the victim's name.

Data breaches are a channel of identity theft: a company that holds customer information can be hacked and personal details exposed; FTC guidance after a breach notice is to act quickly — change passwords, especially reused ones, and use extra login security.

Phishing is a channel of identity theft: fraudulent emails, texts, or calls pose as a legitimate company to trick people into revealing information; FTC guidance is that when an unexpected message asks you to act, contact the company through a phone number or website you know is real.

Stolen mail is a channel of identity theft: statements and bills carry personal information, so FTC guidance is to take mail out of the mailbox as soon as possible, and a stopped bill can mean a thief changed the billing address.

Card skimmers are a channel of identity theft: illegal card readers attached to payment terminals copy the data on a card's magnetic stripe, and the theft is often discovered only when a statement or overdraft notice shows unauthorized charges.

The classic warning signs of identity theft are unexpected bills and charges, unfamiliar accounts (visible on credit reports), withdrawals you did not make, and being denied credit; the CFPB adds small test withdrawals, inquiries from companies you never contacted, and debt-collector calls about debts that are not yours.

When a company denies an application based on your credit report, federal rules entitle you to a free copy of that report (within 60 days); a thief's accounts on the file can cause legitimate applications to be denied. Stated as general guidance, not legal advice.

Protection is general practice: strong passwords plus two-factor authentication where available, shredding documents with personal information, taking mail promptly, and guarding the Social Security number by asking why an organization needs it.

A credit freeze blocks new credit accounts from being opened in your name, is free to place and lift, and does not affect your credit score; a fraud alert makes businesses verify your identity before granting new credit and lasts one year, renewable, with one bureau notifying the other two.

The FTC's recovery path when identity theft happens: report the theft at IdentityTheft.gov to get a free personal recovery plan; contact companies where fraud occurred and close or freeze the affected accounts; place a fraud alert and freeze; and review credit reports for fraudulent accounts.

Identity theft and credit are linked: accounts a thief opens in your name, and the debts left unpaid, can appear on your credit reports and hurt your own applications; the report itself is the sibling topic credit-reports.

Honest framing: protection steps reduce risk but cannot guarantee safety, and a thief obtaining your information is a crime of access, not evidence that the victim trusted the wrong person or did something wrong.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the victim is at fault when identity theft happens.
positions: Popular assumption: the victim must have shared information or trusted the wrong person.
FTC material treats identity theft as a crime where the thief gains access without permission; protection steps minimize risk but cannot guarantee safety.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the honest framing: identity theft is a crime of access, not of trust; the victim's behavior is not on trial, and acting fast is what limits damage.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a credit freeze freezes everything, including existing cards.
positions: Some believe a freeze locks all credit activity, including purchases on existing cards.
FTC states a freeze prevents new credit accounts from being opened and does not affect the credit score; existing accounts keep working, and the freeze can be lifted temporarily.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the freeze's actual scope: new credit accounts are blocked, existing accounts are unaffected, and the freeze is free to place and lift.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where the dispute mechanics belong between sibling topics.
positions: The credit-reports sibling topic owns the dispute process in detail.
Recovery guidance names disputing as one of the FTC's steps after theft.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names dispute as a step and points to credit-reports for the mechanics; no duplication of the process.

sourceRecords.title: What To Know About Identity Theft
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Backbone Tier A source. Provides the working definition (identity theft is when someone uses your personal or financial information without your permission), the information targeted, what thieves do with it (buy things, open credit cards and utility accounts), the warning-sign list (stopped bills, unexpected charges and bills, withdrawals, unrecognized accounts), protection practices (credit freeze, fraud alert, shredding, prompt mail pickup, asking questions before giving the SSN, two-factor authentication), and recovery (report at IdentityTheft.gov for a free personal recovery plan).

sourceRecords.title: What is identity theft? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Tier A. Frames identity theft as occurring when someone steals your identity to commit fraud — using personal information without permission; lists what thieves may do (rent apartments, get credit cards, receive government benefits or tax refunds, open other accounts in your name); points to IdentityTheft.gov as the federal one-stop resource; page explicitly states it is general consumer information, not legal advice.

sourceRecords.title: How to tell if someone is using your identity
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. FTC consumer alert. States that protection steps minimize risk but a thief can get information anyway; signs include credit accounts and inquiries you don't recognize, purchases and withdrawals you didn't make, tax-return and unemployment fraud, and medical services you didn't receive. Anchors the honest framing that theft can happen despite precautions.

sourceRecords.title: How can I spot identity theft? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Tier A. Warning-sign detail: charges or withdrawals you did not make (even a small one can be a test before a larger theft), reviewing free credit reports, inquiries from companies you've never contacted, and not ignoring debt-collector calls about debts that are not yours. Page states it is general consumer information, not legal advice.

sourceRecords.title: Have you been affected by a data breach? Read on
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. FTC consumer alert on the data-breach channel: hackers exploit reused passwords; after a breach notice, act quickly — change the exposed password and similar ones, use a password manager, add extra login security — and IdentityTheft.gov has next steps for exposed information.

sourceRecords.title: Watch out for card skimming at the gas pump
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. FTC consumer alert defining skimmers as illegal card readers attached to payment terminals that grab data off a card's magnetic stripe without the user's knowledge; criminals sell the data or use it to buy things online; victims often learn only from a statement or overdraft notice.

sourceRecords.title: Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Tier A. Credit freeze: nobody can open a new credit account in your name while it is in place, free to place and lift, does not affect your credit score, anyone can freeze any time, liftable temporarily. Fraud alerts: businesses must verify identity before granting new credit; initial alert lasts one year and is renewable; the bureau contacted must tell the other two.

sourceRecords.title: How to recover from identity theft
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. FTC consumer alert naming the recovery steps: call the companies where fraud occurred (close or freeze accounts, change logins, passwords, and PINs), place a fraud alert and get free credit reports (freeze too), and report identity theft to the FTC at IdentityTheft.gov for a free personal recovery plan.

sourceRecords.title: What do I do if I am a victim of identity theft? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Tier A. CFPB recovery guidance: close compromised accounts, report the theft at IdentityTheft.gov, place fraud alerts or security freezes on credit reports, and take steps to protect credit; fraud alerts require creditors to verify it is really you before opening a new account, issuing an additional card, or raising a limit.
